questions.question: What is mypy and how do you use it for static type checking in Python?
questions.title: mypy: Static Type Checking for Python
questions.direct_answer: mypy is a static type checker for Python: it reads your type annotations and reports type errors before you run the code, catching bugs that Python's runtime ignores (passing a str where an int is expected, calling a missing method, returning the wrong type). You run it on your files (mypy file.py) or package (mypy mypackage/); it reports errors like 'Argument 1 has incompatible type.' mypy doesn't change runtime behavior — Python still ignores annotations at runtime; mypy checks them statically. Use it in CI and your editor to get the safety of static typing without giving up Python's dynamic nature.

sections.title: The Static Enforcement Layer
sections.content: mypy is a static type checker for Python: it reads your type annotations and reports type errors before you run the code, catching bugs that Python's runtime ignores — passing a str where an int is expected, calling a method that doesn't exist, returning the wrong type. You run it on a file (mypy file.py) or a package (mypy mypackage/), and it reports errors like 'Argument 1 has incompatible type.' mypy doesn't change runtime behavior — Python still ignores annotations at runtime; mypy is the static layer that enforces them. Use it in CI (run on every commit) and in your editor (live checks) to get the safety of static typing without giving up Python's dynamic nature. Fix the errors it reports — annotations only help if the errors they flag are fixed.

sections.title: mypy's Place in the Workflow
sections.content:
mypy reads annotations and reports errors; Python ignores them at runtime. Run it in CI and the editor.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S[annotated source] --> M[mypy: static check]
  M -->|errors| E[fix before running]
  S -->|runtime| R[Python: ignores annotations]
  E --> R
```

sections.title: Running mypy and an error it catches
sections.content:
```python
# example.py
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hi, {name}!"

greet(123)        # BUG: passing an int where str is expected

# --- Run mypy ---
# $ mypy example.py
#   example.py:4: error: Argument 1 to "greet" has incompatible type "int";
#   expected "str"  [arg-type]
#
# Python RUNS this fine (no runtime error) — mypy catches it BEFORE running.
#
# Common mypy commands:
#   mypy file.py             # check one file
#   mypy mypackage/          # check a package
#   mypy --strict mypackage/ # stricter checks (recommended for new code)
#   mypy --ignore-missing-imports  # don't fail on untyped third-party libs
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Thinking annotations are enforced at runtime — Python ignores them; mypy is the enforcement layer.
Running mypy once and ignoring its output — it only helps if you fix the flagged errors.
Not configuring mypy (strict mode, ignores) — the defaults are lenient; --strict catches more.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: mypy is a static type checker: it reads annotations and reports type errors BEFORE running.
Python ignores annotations at runtime — mypy is the static enforcement layer.
Run it on files/packages (mypy file.py, mypy mypackage/); use --strict for new code.

Fix the errors it reports — annotations only help if the flagged errors are fixed.
